This was a good idea squandered into a mind-numbingly boring game.

The basic premise is that you’re the head of the student council as an extremely prestigious high-class private school and you’ve been tasked with keeping order. You investigate rumours and manage events and in the process protect the school’s reputation. To investigate, you send out the other members of the student council to interact with students. There are also overarching plots, such as sussing out a traitor among your own.

Unfortunately the game is just a long series of skill checks. You send someone to investigate, and they either fail and don’t find anything or pass and get you the info you need to progress. There’s no deduction gameplay at all. Further, I was really disappointed to find that the plotlines are all repeatable and RNG-based. So like, the traitor on the council is selected randomly, and while they each have reasons for being the traitor when they’re selected, this means there’s no actual story thruline or consequences since it’s all random. The cases you have to investigate are interesting until you realize they, too, repeat ad nauseum. The result is nothing matters. You either pass or fail skill checks which get you repeated information. At a certain point you can even just skip some of the skill checks since you know how the cases play out since there’s so few and they’re constantly repeating.

Part of me wants to say it plays like a board game — roll skill checks, turn over cards to see solutions if you pass — but this doesn’t really explain the lack of deduction elements; there are a litany of board game with this kind of gameplay that also require thought from the player.

The only actual gameplay involves managing the stress level of the council members, who can only be sent out so many consecutive rounds. Additionally, some of them will refuse to do certain tasks. You can raise relationship levels with them to increase their max stress level, but only for the first few weeks of the gameplay — after the first major game over check in week 5, you’re locked into a romance plotline with one of them and then all you can do is hang out with that one over and over for no extra stat boosts.

I was even more disappointed to find that training council member skills doesn’t carry over between games, which is baffling. The extra skills points you get are so thin on the ground they’re almost irrelevant in the face of the insanely high mid-to-late-game checks (in retrospect what I should have done was loaded them all on one character instead of trying to balance them), but I figured it was geared toward accumulating them over many runs, so that you could gradually see and do more and more. But… no. I don’t even know why they’re there.

I was insanely bored by this game about an hour into it, but figured I’d see it through one school-year playthrough just for completion’s sake. I got about 2/3 through semi-paying-attention before forgetting to wrap up a story mission and hitting a game over. And I really just don’t care enough to go back and replay.

It´s a fun and interesting game that I definitely recommend but know that the plot got progressively less interesting for me. 
The writing is really solid, surprisingly so. I´m a writer myself and have generally very annoyingly high standards and this game fully sold me on the characters and the setting. It has some of the best "awkwardly getting to know someone" dialogue I have ever seen. It has the most interesting take on a "mysterious" type girl I have seen in a long time and from what little I was able to see from the other girls, they were all super solid, fun and interesting. I really liked the character I got to play as, even if I wasn´t able to name her. She was convincingly strong and ruthless. I really enjoyed the choices you get to make in the game as well as the gameplay. I don´t regret buying this game, it was a fun experience!
That being said, I´m just not finishing this game. My biggest critique is that [spoiler] after the harvest festival, the game decides that you´re done with talking to other people and makes you talk to one girl forever. It´s miserable because I really enjoyed the variety from before. The game also tries to sell you on a frankly quite poorly done mystery. I feel like the writer themself wasn´t very enthusiastic about writing this part and felt insecure about some of the plot holes. I would recommend the whole “write a story you´d want to read” thing for their next game because they´re clearly very talented but I feel like they just kind of went with the first idea and weren´t very enthusiastic about it.
I feel like the game made so many interesting points about this elite school that cares about its reputation and how that cultivates isolation and incompetence in terms of teaching kids about household chores and how it can discourage fun and individuality and breeds hostility and gossiping and judgement and how extreme the staff can be to protect the school and not the students- and yet all these rich people are still human being that try to be kind! But then the plot is that one stalker in a spooky mask threatens to harm only one girl and then they don´t even kill her.
I would have cared way more if a whole group showed up, all wearing masks, and if they threatened the student body in general, saying they would poison the lunches or something.
There were so many more interesting choices that could have been made here. 
I´m annoying so here is a more interesting plot:
What if the community surrounding this rich school caused them problems? Maybe there is poverty in the community and there was a protest or something and it makes the school crack down even further on students being able to leave. Maybe people start going a little stir crazy.
And if you want a mystery, what if every two months a different girl became a traitor? What if the school slowly became more and more violent, seemingly for no reason? What if people kept disappearing and then reappearing with nobody acknowledging that they were ever gone, including the students themselves? Hell, what if the mask society was a group of angry, abused communist students that are threatening to put a bomb under the school? [/spoiler]
It just didn´t live up to the quality of the previous writing and that´s okay, like I said, I have really high standards and I´m also not a teenager. Maybe I´m not the target audience here.

If you can get past the 'girl-on-girl action' fetish (because what else goes on in an all-girls school, right?), there's actually a robust detective/strategy game in there.

The mysteries feel like mysteries.
You have to send the girls out to investigate rooms, interrogate witnesses or suspects, stake out areas, follow people or just throw some weight around to solve them.
They all have various stats that are used against opponent stats to see if they succeed or fail. There's RNG, but it's very controllable. You don't know the opponent's stats, whether room or person, until after you attempt something at least once. After that, you know just how tough they are and you can assign girls better suited for the task, if needed.

Meanwhile, there's the romantic subplot going on with you either seducing or being seduced by the girls. Which can influence how well they get the jobs done. Especially since one of them is working against you and you have to figure out which one. Then use your (ahem) 'charms' to confront them.

I tend to just ignore the subplot and play it mostly for the mysteries. And with different mysteries each playthrough, there's plenty of replayability. Although the subplot cutscenes and seduction visual novel elements can slow the gameplay down considerably.

You can also change the characters in the game, but it'll still refer to them as girls. So this may end up a bit awkward unless you make them all female.

Overall, a good mystery game with some strategy elements, wrapped up with a romantic visual novel subplot that's not too hard to ignore or bypass if it doesn't interest you.

From the creator of Long Live the Queen comes an all-girls Catholic boarding school simulator. Compared to all of the other games in the Hanako library, it's probably the most systems-driven, which I love: it's by far the most replayable game, in part because the identity of the traitor is randomized, and in each playthrough, you'll have to ferret out who they are through clever deduction -- did your minion fail their task because of a bad dice roll, or did they botch things on purpose?

This mechanic, and many others, lead to an experience where the game's themes are woven into the gameplay mechanics: the game is partly about paranoia, and it achieves this not by having a character monologue at you about paranoia, but by giving you a gameplay mechanic that causes you to distrust your minions. The game has interesting things to say about how people in authority abuse power, but it never beats you over the head with its message; the game is simply content to give you absolute power over the student body (with more than a few "dirty tricks" that you can use when expediency is more important than the approval of the student body), and it leaves you to your own devices. You could question people politely, and doing so will prevent you from unfairly detaining innocents...but skipping to aggressive interrogation will save you time, and sometimes, you have too many cases to close and not enough resources. Something's got to give, and if that "something" isn't going to be your clearance rate, well...

Black Closet has a very clear "tabletop" theme, giving you the satisfying, tactile sound of D20's rolling on a wooden table each time you perform an action that requires a stat check. That randomization is inherently a part of the game, which turns it into a game that's not about achieving 100% success, but about playing the odds and doing the best you can with the resources that you're given. These elements may not appeal to everyone, but they scratch me exactly where I itch, and they feed perfectly into the game's themes of paranoia and uncertainty.  (If you're the kind of person who gets excited by the idea of "pareto-optimization," then you too will probably like these mechanics for the same reason I did.)  There's a demo available on the developer's website, which should give you a feel for the overall vibe of the game to see if it gels with you.

Black Closet it a stat boosting style "choices matter" game. Compared with Long Live the Queen, the play style is quite different, looking almost like a board game, where you have to make card combinations and put them into your executive tray each day (up to 5 actions). Additionally, it's much easier to track the point threshholds needed to achieve certain tasks. 

Game play is never exactly the same, save for key events in the main story. The "cases" you get outside of main story look repetitive, but even two cases that start out reading very similarly at the start can have different outcomes (e.g., [spoiler]missing supply cases could end up in someone having stolen supplies, the supplies being delivered to the wrong classroom, or the supplies never having been ordered[/spoiler]). The trick to the cases is finding the ideal sequence of investigation to help tease out which outcome the case has, while minimizing your Karma/Reputation loss. 

I enjoy the board game look/play feel of this game, and the ambient music definitely sets a mood.

It's a puzzle and a mystery, and very difficult. But you should face the challenge and see it through to the end.

BAD: Horribly clumsy UI, repetitive cases with insipid solving mechanism, unrewarding gameplay, carte blanche protagonist.

This game is a visual novel with slight RPG elements (character stats, dice rolls to determine investigation results) and elementary tactical elements (resource management). You play as Elsa, a student council head with three goals: keep the school's (and the student council's) reputation intact by solving weekly cases that threaten to cause commotion; win the loyalty and perhaps affection of your student council members; and find which one of them is actually a traitor (and who's behind it).

Game can only be saved at the beginning of each week. Unfortunately the weekly investigation phases -- where 90% of the game time is spent -- lose their appeal after a couple of hours. They are always based on deduction via trial and error, often requiring either several attempts or blind luck to solve in the given time. The basic investigation mechanism is always the same, select a character and test her skill against an opposing value. Often the cases drag on and on, overlapsing new cases. The same cases also get recycled several times during a single play-through with only minor variation to details, The rewards and grades for solved cases seem to be rather arbitrary.

Relationships are advanced via short sequences that allow interaction with the student council members. Early in the game you can interact with any two members on weekends, later you need to select only one member for the rest of the game and lose the ability to initiate contact with all the others. Sometimes a member will initiate a meeting with you during the week. Unfortunately this relationship aspect also comes a bit short. Other characters are varied and have interesting stories, but because I didn't know anything about my own character at the beginning of the game, and didn't have any real dialogue of my own during it (protagonist only gets to choose from brief options), I did not feel any connection with my character, there was no immersion. Further, this lack of own voice lead to very forced and unnatural dialogue from the other characters, as they had to fill me in on my own history. And unlike in normal visual novels, going through all character routes would be a herculean task.

I don't often complain of a game being too long, but that is the case here. I was completely fed up solving the carbon copy cases long before the first play-through ended after ~10 hours. However, it turned out that the end mission is impossible unless you build your team from the very beginning in a certain way. Completing the game would require another play-through, And of course seeing the other romance options would also require multiple play-throughs. I love this game and wholeheartedly recommend it. The gameplay is simple and mostly intuitive, but has enough variety and moving parts to keep you guessing and keep things fun.

This game has a bit of a rough learning curve, with already convoluted cases being complicated by the presence of a traitor working against you. That being said, once you start to get a feel for what interactions are helpful in what situations, the traitor adds another level of depth and intrigue to this fantastic game - did my trusted lieutenant Vonne really fail to spot anything in the boiler room, or is she actively working against me? Is the silent and mysterious Rowan being outplayed in a game of cat and mouse, or is she *trying* to get me caught? Just what is her motivation, anyway?

The writing, though, is where the game truly shines. It is, at times, witty and fun, tense and unnerving, gentle and sensual. The balance between solving the mysteries of the school and reaching out to your allies without ever truly knowing who you can trust is amazing. It perfectly evokes the feeling of being young and in love in a big, uncertain world.

In the end, how you handle those pressures really does matter. If you close yourself off or become hostile to try to force answers out of people, or even just to try to keep things running smoothly, you may find yourself in a situation where no one is willing to help you. If you let your paranoia get to you, you can even end up hurting those close to you. 

I was stunned when, playing through Rowan's path a second time, I treated her a little bit differently and ended up going down an entirely different path with her. I expected maybe a different, less happy ending tacked on, but I ended up seeing an entirely different side of her, and pushed her to change in entirely different ways. This game has a ton of depth and responds to your choices more than you may think.

I truly enjoyed this game. I can't recommend it enough. It is definitely worth giving a try. If you can stick with it through the (admittedly rough) learning curve, you'll be rewarded with an unforgettable story of intrigue and romance. You won't regret it.

I'm a huge fan of this game, and have been meaning to review it forever. The art style is unique and charming, the mood and music are awesome, the game mechanics are deceptively simple and novel, the story is cool, the characters feel layered and distinct, and the dialog is very well-crafted and flexible.

I have actually bought this game for a few people over the years because I think there are so many different things to like: part visual novel, part tabletop, part mystery.

The gist of this game is you're the student council president at an all-girls private school. You're in charge or resolving conflicts and drama between students. Your ultimate goal is to protect the reputation of the school and improve your standings for college applications. Your student council team uses a mix of social and reconnaissance skills (which you can level up as you see fit) in order to get to the bottom of various scandals and crises. Each situation has multiple possible resolutions, some more dire than others - your job is to prioritize risk and play damage control. It's a pretty fun mix of role playing and simulation, which runs parallel to a more visual novel style game about bonding with your council members (yes, like that, but not like *that*.)

Honestly, one of the best parts of this game is how not only do you have tons of dialog options to really make your character speak for you, but the game generally doesn't punish you for being yourself. You can work in flavor answers instead of the "right" answer and still reach the same general plot conclusions. Also, if an answer backfires, you can scroll back in the scene as far as you want and choose other answers. I like this for a couple reasons - one, you shouldn't have to reload the game just because your answer didn't work like you thought it would. Two, there are so many little bits and pieces of good dialog spread throughout the game that having to replay 20 times to read it all would be excessive, and this lets you feel things out a little more in one playthrough (while still leaving room to replay and choose other answers if that is indeed how you prefer to play.)

Concerning the dialog and characters, I love the way they're written. Characters have predominant characteristics you'll quickly come to know them by, but they all have their own layers, and you can start to feel for how different dialog options will affect them. Some take jokes better than others, and you can tell crossing certain lines might provoke rather than convince. Getting to learn how to reason with, connect with, inspire or understand each character has its own flavor. There are a few curves thrown in, too, and room for experimentation and surprises (you can look at the locked achievements for hints about these!)

Some people will find this game repetitive, but for me, I was able to pick it back up right after beating it and start a new path up out of curiosity for what other directions the story could have gone. I guess one criticism about this is that most of the story dialog happens in the first half of the game. Things start to dry up more toward the end, where most of the chips have fallen and you've already gotten to know your team of characters. Also, if you manage to derail yourself from whatever relationship-based plot path you were on, the story scenes will kind of just disappear and you have to assume you botched things somehow. This isn't a huge problem, but it does stand out a little.

I love the various elements at play in the story and tone. You stand as a force of order and rationality, and indeed everything seems to be realistic and has a logical explanation to be found, yet the sinister undertones of the game, just like imagination and unseen machinations in real life, can tempt you to doubt yourself and your senses. There are fringes of the theatrical or the bizarre here and there without ever crossing the line into fantasy.

One mixed feeling I have is about the traitor mechanic. Without spoiling it, I'll just say t's a great idea, and the first time you play, it's an interesting concern to try and figure out. Once you understand how it works in practice, it is a bit more plain on subsequent plays - narratively it's still great, but there could have been a little bit more going on in the game mechanism aspect of it for replays.

I would love to see a similar game to this, whether a sequel or just a spiritual successor. Maybe for me this is just lightning in a bottle, but I can totally get into this haunting, calculating, erudite and intimate microgenre. Credit to the developers, for sure, because this artfully assembled game certainly feels like more than just the sum of its unique parts.

First of all, I am generally a big fan of Hanako Games, and while this one is a departure from many of the others I've palyed, it is still a very good game.

I expected a VN based on my experience with their games, and while it does have a lot in common with one, it isn't really one. It's more of a strategy game with what I think of as visual novel "cutscenes" with choices on the weekends and during pivotal moments.

Overall, this is definitely more of a strategy/puzzle game in the mystery genre. Each week, you receive various cases, and as the head of the Student Council, you are essentially the lead detective for these cases. You assign various girls to complete tasks based on their stats and the stats required for the mission, and there is a dice roll element as well to add some unpredictability. Tasks include things like interviewing or accusing suspects, searching rooms, and conducting stakeouts.

Of course, you can also choose to pursue one of the girls romantically or as a friend  during the course of your sleuthing. There is also a lot of replay value if you want to chase all the achievements, but good luck doing it without a strategy guide as some of them are time-dependent or based on careful stat-raising of certain girls fairly early on (or colossal luck, if you didn't stat-raise correctly before getting into the "main" storyline mysteries - some of them have REALLY high checks comparative to what you really need to solve most smaller cases successfully).

PROS:
Interesting concept
Lots of replay value
Nice art
Multiple endings
Romantic and friendship routes
Unique gameplay
VN-esque, even if it really isn't one

CONS:
Can get repetitive
No voice acting
